tagline: Israel's story retold from Adam to David for a small, returned people, asking whether God's promises to David and his temple still stand.
overview:
First Chronicles is the first half of a single work (Chronicles was one book in the Hebrew Bible and was divided in two by the Greek translators) that retells Israel's history from Adam to the return from exile in Babylon. The first nine chapters are genealogies: long family lists that run from Adam through the nations, through Abraham and Jacob's twelve sons, down to the people who resettled Jerusalem after the exile. Then the book tells one reign in detail. Saul falls in a single chapter, and the rest of the book belongs to David: his anointing at Hebron, his mighty men, the capture of Jerusalem, the bringing of the ark of the covenant (the gold-covered chest that stood for God's throne among his people) to the city, God's promise of an everlasting dynasty, David's wars, and above all his preparations for the temple his son Solomon will build.

Readers who come from Samuel and Kings notice at once that much is missing and much is added. The Chronicler (the name scholars give the anonymous author) leaves out David's adultery with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, and Absalom's revolt, and he adds long lists of priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and officials. This is not a cover-up, since his readers had Samuel and Kings in hand. It is a second telling with a different question. Samuel and Kings, finished during the exile, explain why the kingdom fell. Chronicles, written after the return, asks who the people of God are now and whether the promises still hold.

That is why the book matters. It was written for a small community living in the ruins of a great past, without a king, under a foreign empire, gathered around a modest rebuilt temple. Chronicles tells them that they are the continuation of all Israel, that God's promise to David was never withdrawn, and that the worship of God at his house is the center of their life. It is history written as a sermon to people who wondered if they still mattered.
author: The book does not name its author. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud credits Ezra, the priest and scribe of the return, and for a long time many scholars held that one author (the Chronicler) wrote both Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah, partly because the last verses of 2 Chronicles are repeated as the first verses of Ezra. Since the late 1960s and 1970s, many scholars, notably Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson, have argued from differences in language and outlook that Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah come from different hands, though others still see a close connection. Most agree that the author belonged to the circle of the Jerusalem temple and cared deeply about the Levites, the singers, and the right ordering of worship. Some suggest he was himself a Levite, but that is an inference, not a fact. The writer names many sources, including the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the seer (1 Chronicles 29:29), and he clearly used the books of Samuel and Kings in a form close to the one we have.
date: Chronicles was written after the exile. It ends with Cyrus king of Persia allowing the Jews to return (2 Chronicles 36:22-23), an event of 539/538 BC, and the royal line in 1 Chronicles 3 runs several generations past Zerubbabel, who led the return around 520 BC. First Chronicles 29:7 counts gold in darics, a Persian coin first minted under Darius I in the late sixth century BC. Most scholars date the book in the Persian period, commonly between about 400 and 350 BC. Some argue for an earlier first edition around the time the temple was rebuilt (about 520 to 515 BC), and a smaller group places it in the early Greek period after Alexander the Great, around 300 BC or a little later. The exact decade can't be fixed, but the book's world is clearly Jerusalem under Persian rule.
setting: When Chronicles was written, the kingdom of David was centuries gone. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC and carried many of its people into exile. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon and allowed exiled peoples to return home and rebuild their shrines. A minority of Jews returned. The temple was rebuilt and dedicated around 515 BC, and in the next century Ezra and Nehemiah worked to reform the community and restore Jerusalem's walls. Judah (called Yehud in Persian records) was now a small province of the Persian Empire, governed by officials answerable to the Great King. There was no Davidic king on the throne, though David's descendants were still known by name. The community lived by the law of Moses, gathered around the temple, and argued about who truly belonged to Israel. Chronicles speaks into all of that: its genealogies, its lists of temple servants, and its picture of a united Israel gathered around David are addressed to readers who needed to know their place in the story.
purpose: Chronicles was written to give a restored but diminished community its identity and its hope. The genealogies tell them they are not a new people but the continuation of Israel, rooted all the way back to Adam and including all twelve tribes, even those long scattered. The account of David and Solomon shows what Israel is at its best: a people united under the king God chose, worshiping at the house God chose, in the way God ordered. The book also teaches a pattern its readers could act on. Kings and people who seek the LORD find him; those who forsake him are forsaken. Repentance is always possible, and prayer at God's house is always heard. The Chronicler is less interested in explaining the past than in calling his own generation to faithful worship and to trust that God's promise to David still stands.
story: Chronicles comes after the whole story of Israel's monarchy has already been told in Samuel and Kings, and it retells that story from a later vantage point. In English Bibles it follows 2 Kings and comes before Ezra and Nehemiah, which pick up where it ends. In the traditional Hebrew order it sits among the Writings, often as the very last book of the Hebrew Bible, so that the Scriptures end with Cyrus's words inviting God's people to go up and rebuild. First Chronicles sweeps from Adam to the eve of Solomon's reign in nine chapters of names and twenty chapters on David. Second Chronicles continues with Solomon's temple and the kings of Judah to the exile and the decree of return.
christ: The heart of 1 Chronicles is God's promise to David in chapter 17: a son whose throne God will establish forever, who will build God's house, and to whom God will be a Father. Chronicles tells the promise in a way that looks past any single king. God says he will set this son over “My house and My kingdom forever” (1 Chronicles 17:14), making the kingdom God's own. The Chronicler wrote when no son of David reigned, so the promise was a hope, not a present fact. The New Testament announces its fulfillment in Jesus, the son of David, whose genealogy in Matthew 1 is built from the same family lines found in 1 Chronicles 2 and 3. Jesus speaks of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21), and the letter to the Hebrews applies the words “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” to him (Hebrews 1:5). The Chronicler's longing for a king who rules for God and a house where God meets his people finds its answer there.
reading: Read Chronicles as theological history: a real account of the past, carefully selected and arranged to preach to its own generation. Keep Samuel and Kings open alongside it, because many of its most important points are made by what it adds, changes, or leaves out. Don't skip the genealogies. They were the book's first word to its readers, and small notes buried in them (a prayer, a crime, a victory, an exile) carry the book's themes. Watch for the words seek and unfaithful, for the phrase all Israel, and for the long attention to Levites and music, which shows what the author thought mattered most. A common misreading treats Chronicles as a whitewash of David. It is better read as a portrait of what God was doing through David, painted for readers who already knew his failures.

structure.title: All Israel in its generations
structure.summary: Genealogies from Adam through the nations to Jacob's twelve sons, with Judah and David's line first, Levi at the center, and a closing list of those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile.

structure.title: The fall of Saul
structure.summary: Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa, and the Chronicler explains that he died for his unfaithfulness, so that the LORD turned the kingdom over to David.

structure.title: David made king by all Israel
structure.summary: All Israel anoints David at Hebron, he captures Jerusalem, and long lists of warriors from every tribe show the whole nation rallying to him.

structure.title: The ark comes to Jerusalem
structure.summary: A first attempt to move the ark ends in Uzza's death; after a three-month pause the Levites carry it properly into the city with music, sacrifice, and a psalm of thanksgiving.

structure.title: God's covenant with David
structure.summary: David wants to build God a house, but God promises instead to build David a house, a dynasty whose son will reign over God's kingdom forever.

structure.title: David's wars and victories
structure.summary: David defeats the surrounding nations and brings their tribute to Jerusalem, securing the peace in which the temple can be built.

structure.title: The census and the temple site
structure.summary: David's census brings a plague on Israel, and the place where the plague stops, the threshing floor of Ornan, becomes the site of the future temple.

structure.title: Preparing for the temple and for Solomon
structure.summary: David gathers materials, charges Solomon, organizes the Levites, priests, singers, gatekeepers, and officials, leads the people in giving, blesses God in prayer, and dies after Solomon is made king.

themes.title: All Israel
themes.body: Chronicles insists that the people of God are all twelve tribes, not only Judah. The genealogies include the northern tribes, the tribes across the Jordan, and even foreigners grafted into Israel's families. The whole nation makes David king, and the whole assembly brings up the ark. For a small community in Judah, this was both a comfort and a challenge: they stood in continuity with the whole people, and the door stayed open for others to return.

themes.title: David's house and God's kingdom
themes.body: The promise of 1 Chronicles 17 governs the book. God will raise up David's son and establish his throne forever. Chronicles presents the Davidic throne as the LORD's own throne and the kingdom as God's kingdom, entrusted to David's line. Written when no Davidic king reigned, the book kept that promise alive as a hope for the future.

themes.title: Worship at the house of God
themes.body: More than any other historical book, Chronicles cares about worship: the ark, the altar, the temple site, the Levites who carry and serve, the singers and musicians, the gatekeepers and treasurers. David is remembered less as a warrior than as the founder of Israel's worship. The book teaches that praise, thanksgiving, and ordered service at God's house are the center of a faithful people's life.

themes.title: Seeking God and unfaithfulness
themes.body: The Chronicler uses a simple and searching vocabulary. To seek the LORD is to turn to him in worship, prayer, and obedience; to be unfaithful is to break faith with him, as Saul did. Seeking brings help and blessing; unfaithfulness brings disaster, as the note about Judah's exile in 1 Chronicles 9:1 shows. The pattern is not mechanical fate but an invitation, because every generation can still seek him.

themes.title: God's hand in history
themes.body: From Adam to David, the book presents history as ruled by God. He turns the kingdom from Saul to David, gives David victory, stirs the hearts of foreign kings, and chooses the place of his house. David's great prayer in chapter 29 gathers this up: the kingdom, the power, and everything in heaven and earth belong to the LORD, and what his people give him has first come from his hand.

keyChapters.why: The genealogies begin with Adam, not Abraham, placing Israel's story inside the story of all humanity and all the nations.
The list of those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile connects the ancient genealogies to the Chronicler's own community and its temple service.
Saul's death is told with a theological verdict: he died for his unfaithfulness, and the LORD turned the kingdom to David.
The first attempt to move the ark ends in Uzza's death, teaching that zeal for God must honor God's holiness and his ordered ways.
The ark arrives in Jerusalem, and David appoints Levites to lead continual praise, with a psalm of thanks that becomes the book's model of worship.
God promises David an everlasting dynasty and a son who will build God's house, the promise that shapes the rest of Chronicles.
David's sinful census leads to the choice of the temple site at Ornan's threshing floor, where judgment is stopped by sacrifice.
David leads Israel in generous giving and offers a great prayer of praise that confesses everything as God's, before Solomon takes the throne.
